newsitem.title: JAPAN: Aluminum- Japan premiums seen peaking this quarter.
newsitem.headline: Aluminum- Japan premiums seen peaking this quarter.

text.p: Japanese premiums for aluminium, driven up by low domestic stocks, are likely to ease in the next quarter as a sales tax increase bites into economic growth, traders said on Friday.
"The premiums for the third quarter should be about $10 lower than now. I would not buy if it's $80," said a trader at a major trading house.
Trading houses and end-users are now getting nervous ahead of next month's negotiations of premiums for deliveries in the third quarter on long-term contracts.

Of Japan's annual aluminium demand of some 2.4 million tonnes, about one-third is sold under long-term contracts, another third in development-related long-term deals, and the remaining third through spot deals.

Against the backdrop of a fall in domestic stocks, spot premiums climbed over the past weeks, with traders citing some deals with a premium of as high as $90 per tonne, well above about $80 in long-term contracts for second quarter deliveries.

Traders said aluminium stocks in Yokohama dropped 36,000 tonnes to 177,700 tonnes at the end of March from the previous month, far below usual levels of well above 200,000 tonnes. Stocks in Nagoya also fell 15,000 tonnes to about 700,000.

In addition to high U.S. premiums, which have attracted flows of metals, domestic aluminium demand has been very strong during the first months of this year ahead of a hike in Japan's sales tax to five percent from three percent on April 1.
"Currently, it's difficult to buy even Russian metals," said a trader at a trading house, adding that usually Russian aluminium is traded with a discount against western metals.
However, traders agreed the strong aluminium demand was unlikely to continue throughout the year, with even bullish traders forecasting an annual growth of a mere few percent.
They expected long term contracts premiums for deliveries in the third quarter were likely to stand below $80.

"I expect the negotiations to turn below $80," said another trader. "There must be some reaction to the strong growth at the beginning this year. Many believe it should turn around in the third quarter."
The construction and the car sectors should suffer a decline following strong growth since late last year, with some signs already evident in slowing housing orders, traders said.
They are now watching the weather over the next few weeks to determine the direction of demand for beverage cans and air conditioners for the summer.
"The market should ease after the beginning of May," said a third trader. "The first quarter growth seems to have been 5-6 percent. But it will slow down. There's no need to panic."
The industry should not expect help from higher public spending this year and capital investment in some sectors, such as personnel handyphone systems, should stabilise, he added.
Another trader said: "In the second half of this year, we will also see an increase in supply. We heard new production at Australia's Boyne island is to start in June."
